title: The anthill
hookLine: a riddle of an anthill that smokes by night and blazes by day: the body (MN 23)
last: THE RAFT — PUT THE RAFT DOWN.

lines: IT SMOKES BY NIGHT, BLAZES BY DAY.
cards: Late one night in a dark forest, a deity lights up the whole grove and gives a monk named Kumara Kassapa a riddle. There's an anthill, the deity says. It smokes by night and blazes by day.
A brahmin said: wise one, take a tool and dig. Digging, the wise one found a bar. Then a bullfrog, a fork in a road, a strainer, a tortoise, a butcher's knife and block, a piece of meat.
And at last, a naga, a serpent. And the brahmin said: leave the naga. Don't harm it.
Honor the naga. Take this riddle to the Buddha, the deity tells him, and remember his answer.

teach.b: MN 23, the Vammika. Kumara Kassapa does what he's told, and the Buddha opens the riddle piece by piece.
The anthill is this body: made of the four elements, born of mother and father, built up of rice and porridge, subject to wearing away and breaking apart.
Smoking by night is lying awake thinking over what you did by day. Blazing by day is acting on those thoughts, in body, speech and mind. The brahmin is the Buddha himself.
The wise one is a disciple in training. The tool is noble wisdom. Digging is effort.
Then, what the digging turns up. The bar is ignorance. The bullfrog is angry despair.
The fork in the road is doubt. The strainer is the five hindrances. The tortoise is the five aggregates, the pieces we take for a self.
The knife and block are the five cords of sense pleasure. The piece of meat is delight and lust. Each one: lift it out, throw it away.

teach.h: AT THE BOTTOM, A NAGA TO HONOR.
teach.b: And the naga is a monk whose taints are destroyed: leave it, honor it.
So you dig through layer after layer, the plain, heavy stuff of a mind, and at the bottom you don't find a monster. You find something to honor.
The commentary says Kumara Kassapa later reached awakening by working with this very riddle. It was given to a monk still in training, and it took him all the way.

how: Theravada teachers sometimes use the anthill riddle to teach the hindrances and the aggregates, and in the Pali discourses naga, a serpent or great elephant, is also an image for an awakened one.

o: a riddle about the body, dug layer by layer
a picture of a busy, crowded community
a mound where the Buddha first sat to meditate

games.q: match each piece of the riddle to its meaning.

s: at the bottom of the anthill is a monster to destroy
it's a naga, and the brahmin says to leave it and honor it.
the brahmin in the riddle stands for the Buddha
and the wise one is a disciple in training.
the tortoise stands for the five aggregates
the pieces we take for a self.

games.q: digging the anthill, you finally uncover a naga, a serpent. what does the brahmin say to do?
o: leave the naga; honor the naga
games.why: leave it and honor it. everything else is lifted out; the naga stands for one whose taints are destroyed.

practice: Feel the anthill, this body sitting here, built of food and breath, and notice whether it's smoking: thoughts from last night, plans from today, still turning over.
Then dig gently, one layer, a fork in the road of doubt or a bullfrog of irritation, and just name what you find, lifting it out on an out-breath.

wordCard.voice: The anthill. A riddle about the body, dug through layer by layer with wisdom, until there's something at the bottom to honor.

orig.note: Pali vammika: an anthill or termite mound, the name of MN 23.

carryVoice: Your line: dig carefully. The tool is wisdom, and the digging is effort. That's day four hundred twenty-one.
